lesson1.title: Creating the IEP with a Team
lesson1.subheadingInUserPaste: Lesson 1.1: Collaboration with Families and Colleagues
lesson1.objective: You will create an individualized education plan (IEP) by collaborating with the team supporting the student with exceptionalities.
concepts: IEP as a collaborative legal document to provide FAPE
Roles of parents, general and special education teachers, district representative, person interpreting evaluations, and student
Provide parent notice, scheduling options, and meaningful participation
First IEP meeting within 30 calendar days after eligibility determination
Initial meeting: review evaluations, strengths, needs, goals, accommodations and placement
Annual review and parents' ability to request meetings sooner
Progress monitoring using work samples, assessments, grades, intervention data, and accommodation effectiveness
Collaboration between general and special education teachers
State/district assessment accommodations, accessibility features, alternative assessment decisions
Student strengths and family voice in present levels and goals
IEP elements: service delivery, academic performance, goals, educational services, program modifications, transition planning, assessments, peer participation

guidedQuestions.prompt: Why is it important for the IEP to include a Least Restrictive Environment (LRE) statement?
options: To determine the student's testing accommodations
To ensure that the student is educated with non-disabled peers as much as possible
To evaluate whether a student needs assistive technology

guidedQuestions.note: The accurate standard is 'to the maximum extent appropriate,' not unconditional full-time general education placement.

Participation with Non-Disabled Peers (LRE)

cautions: WGU's description of who must physically attend every IEP meeting is simplified; lawful team-member excusal and parent-absence exceptions exist.
Federal transition planning generally starts by the IEP effective by age 16 at the latest; state rules may require an earlier age.
WGU's reference to 'fourteen' IDEA disability categories needs careful verification before treating that number as a legal fact.
A three-year reevaluation is the usual maximum interval unless parent and agency agree it is unnecessary, and can occur earlier.
